Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Omar: yeah, i liked the playing part, especially when everyone tried the G-to-D change together. the issue was that three students were still tuning while you were explaining the finger numbers, so they missed the setup. maybe put the tuning reference on the board before people come in? also, the clip-on tuner on the blue amp kept slipping, so that one might need a new battery or a different spot.

Maya: that's helpful, thx. i'll bring the printed tuning chart on thursday and put it by the door, then ask everyone to tune before we start. i don't want to make tuning sound like a test, though. some of the adults said they're embarrassed when their instrument is out of tune, and i want them to feel okay asking for help.

Lena: from the front desk side, the chart could go on the music stand beside the sign-in sheet. people usually stop there to write their name and check which room they're in. we can add a small note that says, “ask us if you want help tuning,” but i can print it only if you send the wording by wednesday afternoon.

Maya: perfect, i'll send it tomorrow. one other piece of Omar's feedback was that i corrected the same two people several times while the rest of the group waited. i didn't notice how much time that took. would it work if i set up pairs for the first exercise, so everyone can try the chord change instead of watching me go around one at a time?

Omar: pairs might help, but i'd keep the groups flexible. the two newer players next to each other both asked me afterward what a “clean” chord should sound like, and neither could tell if they were muting a string. maybe demo the sound first, then have partners listen for one thing at a time. not a whole checklist right away.

Dev: +1 on one listening goal. when i taught the Saturday ukulele group, we used “all four strings ring” as the check, and beginners could hear that without knowing the chord names yet. for guitar, you could choose the three strings that matter for the G shape you're using. might be easier than asking them to judge the whole sound.

Maya: good point. i use the open G shape with the third finger on the low E string, so i'll make sure we're all using the same version. there are a couple of diagrams in the beginner packet, and one shows a different fingering. i can flag the page instead of reprinting the whole packet. does anyone know if the spare copies are still in cabinet 2?

Lena: yep, i counted eight copies in cabinet 2 this morning. four have the older diagram, though, and the sticker on the folder says “revise before copying.” i'll check with Rosa before we hand any out. we also have a stack of blank staff paper there, if you'd rather draw one chord shape on the board and have students mark their own packet.

Maya: i'll draw it on the board for this week, thanks. i also want to answer the comment about the room feeling crowded. we had nine people plus me, and the folding chairs were in a half circle around the amp. would moving the amp toward the window make it easier for people to hear each other, or would that just send the sound into the hallway?

Omar: the amp by the window should be fine if you keep the volume low. the hallway door was open during the lesson, so that was part of the noise, and the piano class next door started five minutes early. i wouldn't move the chairs too close to the wall, though; one person needs space for the left-handed guitar, and the instrument cases take up more floor than we expect.

Maya: right, i'll leave the door closed and keep a clear strip along the wall for cases. for the opening, here's what i'm thinking:
1) sign in and tune with the chart available
2) i'll play the G chord once, slowly, and show the finger placement
3) partners listen for the three selected strings before we switch to the D chord

Omar: that sounds clear. small thought: give them a minute to try the chord on their own before they pair up. last time, the quieter students waited for a partner to tell them what to do. and when you demonstrate, maybe count in with the metronome at 60 bpm; the quick example was hard to follow from the back chairs.

Maya: yes, i'll add a solo minute and set the metronome to 60 bpm for the demo. i can put it on the table rather than the amp, since the amp's little shelf is wobbly. i'm not sure whether the battery in the metronome is fresh, so i'll test it at home and bring the spare just in case.

Priya: one more thing from the feedback form: someone wrote that they wanted a short printed practice plan, but didn't say how much time they have between lessons. could we ask at the end whether people want a five-minute or fifteen-minute version? i don't want to promise a handout every week if that adds a bunch of prep for you.

Maya: that's fair. i'll ask which version they'd use, and i'll make it clear that it's optional. for this week, i can send a short note with the G-to-D exercise and a reminder to stop if their fingertips hurt. should i post that in the class channel after the lesson, or would email be better for the people who aren't in slack?

Lena: email will reach everyone, and i can include the room number for next week because we're in Studio B, not Studio A. i'll send you the current class list, but please don't include the students' personal addresses in the channel post. if you share a general update in slack too, just keep it to the practice note and the schedule.

Dev: did you stay-stitch the cap? velvet can shift a bit, especially if you handle it a lot.

Lee: maybe baste it by hand first and check it on the actor before changing the pattern? also, have you tried easing from the center notch out toward each end?

Luis: I can look at the route export. The stop was grouped with the West Market deliveries, and the map pin is currently on the Cedar Street loading bay. Evan: One detail from the store side: the chilled totes left the shop at 7:42, and the driver scanned all 14 bags at pickup. The “keep upright” label is on the olive oil box, not a glass bottle. The order was packed normally, as far as I can see.

Maya: Got it. I’m also seeing two delivery windows on the customer’s receipt: 8:00–9:00 in the confirmation email and 8:30–9:30 in the text reminder. Has anyone seen whether the schedule changed after the order was placed? I don’t want to give support the wrong window.

Priya: The order history says the customer chose 8:00–9:00 on Tuesday. I don’t see an edit after that. The text reminder was sent at 6:05 this morning, and it has the later window, so there may be a mismatch in the reminder template. I can flag that separately.

Jonah: Small update: the driver marked “customer unavailable” at 8:31, then added a note that the entrance was blocked by a delivery truck. The customer’s message says they were standing by the blue gate at 8:26. Those could both be true if the driver was still at the Cedar Street entrance.

Maya: Could someone check whether the route screen records which entrance note was displayed? If it only shows the map pin, we’ll need to know that before replying. I’d rather ask the driver what they saw than say the customer’s instructions were missing when we haven’t confirmed it.

Luis: I’m checking the dispatch log now. It shows the stop address as 41 Cedar Street, with “courtyard entrance, Pine Lane” in the delivery-note field. Evan: For the store, the remaining question is whether the chilled bags were returned to the cooler after the first attempt. The pickup scan is clear, but there isn’t a return scan in the order record. I’m not saying they were left in the van; I just can’t verify where they are from this page.

Maya: Here’s what I have so far, so we don’t mix the separate questions together:
1. The order was booked for 8:00–9:00, while the reminder text says 8:30–9:30.
2. The map pin points to Cedar Street, and the notes name the Pine Lane courtyard entrance.
3. The driver logged an unavailable customer and a blocked entrance; the customer said they were at the blue gate.
4. We still need to confirm what appeared on the route screen and where the chilled totes are.

Priya: That summary matches the support history. The customer has now asked whether the groceries can still be delivered today, but they haven’t requested a refund or a replacement. Could someone from dispatch check the driver’s current route and let us know what options we can offer? I’ll hold off on promising a time.
